title: Random forests map South African particulate pollution patterns
summary: A random-forest analysis combined ground stations, satellite data and environmental predictors to estimate daily particulate pollution around Gauteng during 2014–2018. It mapped persistent hotspots and seasonal differences, with lower estimated concentrations in much of the region after 2016. The comparison does not establish a policy effect.
organization: Emory University; Council for Scientific and Industrial Research; North-West University; University of Pretoria

evidence.tested: The model used 9,853 station-day observations from 20 monitors and 40 predictors. Random ten-fold cross-validation gave R² .80 and RMSE 9.40 µg/m³. Predicted winter concentrations were highest; Johannesburg and surrounding areas showed little clear change between 2014–2015 and 2016–2018 while much of the domain decreased.
evidence.unknown: Station-day random folds do not demonstrate transfer to unseen monitoring sites or future years. The model underestimates very high concentrations; top-quintile CV R² was .69. Satellite missingness and correction introduce additional uncertainty. A before/after-policy indicator is itself a model predictor, and the comparison has no causal control or counterfactual. Maps are modeled estimates, not complete ground measurements. No individual health benefit is measured.
evidence.ai_role: Learned tree ensembles infer particulate concentrations from satellite, meteorological, land-use and socioeconomic inputs; the field result is the resulting bounded regional exposure pattern.

source_review.scope: Original ground measurements, integration, random-forest Methods, policy analysis and represented Results actually read.
